blocks.raw: <Note>The Bauhaus was not a style school—it was a pedagogy and philosophy school. It taught principles (integration, reduction, honesty in materials) applicable to any medium. Students learned how to think, not what to copy. The Nazi regime closed it in 1933, but Gropius emigrated and spread Bauhaus principles globally.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Critical distinction: Sullivan said "form follows function." Gropius never used this phrase. Gropius believed art and function are inseparable—integration, not sequence. Also: Don't confuse Gropius's Bauhaus (1919–1928 under him) with Mies's Bauhaus directorship (1930–1933). Each director brought different emphases. Gropius's was experimental and inclusive; Mies's was more austere and geometric.</Warn>

Answer: B (1919). Expect questions about Gropius's foundational vision.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Building-to-Principle Association.** You may see: "The Bauhaus Building in Dessau demonstrates the school's principles through [A] applied ornament and historical style [B] honest materials, functional clarity, and integration of art and technology [C] decorative arts and handcraft only [D] rejection of modernism." Answer: B. You must recognize how buildings manifest philosophy.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Role Clarification.** You may see: "Which of the following best describes Walter Gropius's role in the Bauhaus?" Answer: Founder and first director; set pedagogical philosophy; directed school 1919–1928 (before Meyer and Mies). Expect questions distinguishing Gropius from later directors.</ExamTip>

Answer: Gropius unified art, craft, and industry; rejected the fine art-craft hierarchy; taught thinking over style; emphasized mass production for democratic access. Expect contextual questions.</ExamTip>
